The baby's mother had a complicated pregnancy, which led to early labor. The neonatologist considers the biochemical aspects that could be contributing to the baby's condition, specifically focusing on the surfactant composition in the baby’s lungs. A deficiency in one of the surfactant components is suspected. Which lipid component could be deficient in this preterm newborn, contributing to respiratory distress?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option A: Cardiolipin: or Di phosphatidylglycerol is a major lipid of mitochondrial membrane and extracted from myocardium. Decreased cardiolipin level results in mitochondrial dysfunction, heart failure, hypothyroidism, and myopathies.

 

Option C: Phosphatidyl ethanolamine: or Cephalin is found in bio membranes and possess amphipathic properties.

 

Option D: Phosphatidyl inositol: or PIP2 is present in bio membranes and plays important role in mediation of hormone action on bio membranes and also acts as a second messenger.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC) is the major component of lung surfactant, which reduces surface tension in the alveoli, preventing collapse during exhalation. In preterm babies, surfactant production can be insufficient, leading to respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with abetalipoproteinemia presents with an abnormal blood picture showing acanthocytes, alongside symptoms of hyperkeratosis, acrodermatitis, and hypercholesterolemia. Considering the pathophysiology of abetalipoproteinemia and the patient's symptoms, the abnormal red cell morphology and associated clinical manifestations are most likely due to the malabsorption of which essential nutrient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Linoleic acid

 

Option D:

 

  • The genetic defect might result in malabsorption of two fatty acids given in the options, but only linoleic acid is strictly essential in the diet (EFA).
  • Linoleic acid and linolenic acid cannot be synthesized in the body and have to be provided only in the food, so they are essential fatty acids.
  • Arachidonic acid can be formed from linoleic acid, if the dietary supply of it is sufficient.

 

ABETALIPOPROTEINEMIA:

 

  • All apo-B containing lipoproteins are decreased due to defect in microsomal triglyceride transfer protein → TAG is not incorporated into VLDL and chylomicrons → absence of LDL and no absorption of Fat-soluble vitamins (causing mental and physical retardation).
  • Low Serum triglycerides, cholesterol and phospholipids.
  • Blindness due to degenerative changes in retina.
  • Erythrocytes have spiny projections (acanthocytes).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Ascorbic acid and (B) Folic acid: Absorption of water-soluble vitamins such as ascorbate and folate are not affected.

 

Option C: Arachidonic acid: Due to the genetic defect, malabsorption of arachidonic acid is also affected but it’s not an EFA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Abetalipoproteinemia is a disorder characterized by the malabsorption and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids, due to the inability to properly synthesize and secrete apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins.

 

Linoleic acid is a polyunsaturated fatty acid crucial for maintaining membrane integrity and function, including that of red blood cells. The deficiency in linoleic acid disrupts normal membrane structure, leading to the formation of acanthocytes.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old obese woman visits her primary care physician complaining of recurrent episodes of mild epigastric pain and vomiting, particularly after consuming fatty meals. Physical examination reveals tenderness in the epigastric region. Given the patient's symptoms and risk factors, the physician suspects a biliary tract disorder and refers her for an abdominal ultrasound, which confirms the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder. One of the stones appears to be lodged in the upper part of the bile duct, potentially impacting bile flow and digestion. A gallstone obstructing the upper part of the bile duct would most likely lead to an increase in which of the following?

options.label: B
options.text: Excretion of bile salts & Conjugation of bile acids

options.label: C
options.text: The excretion of fats in the feces

questions.answerText: The excretion of fats in the feces
questions.solutionHtml:
he feces, a condition known as steatorrhea.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: Formation of chylomicrons: Chylomicrons are formed in the intestinal cells to transport absorbed fats, including triglycerides, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins, from the intestines to other parts of the body. Bile duct obstruction does not directly affect chylomicron formation but impacts fat absorption, which indirectly could affect chylomicron content.

 

Option B: Excretion of bile salts & Conjugation of bile acids: Bile salts and bile acids are involved in the emulsification of fats and are recycled via the enterohepatic circulation. While obstruction can lead to decreased bile flow into the intestine, it primarily affects fat absorption rather than the excretion or conjugation of bile components.

 

Option D: Recycling of bile salts: The recycling of bile salts is part of the enterohepatic circulation, where bile salts are reabsorbed from the intestines and returned to the liver. A blockage in the bile duct might disrupt this recycling process, but the more immediate effect is on fat absorption and fecal fat excretion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Gallstones are made up of cholesterol, calcium bilirubinate and bile salts.
  • All the above given details such as female, middle-aged, and overweight shows the patient has gallbladder disease.
  • FUNCTION: The gallbladder stores bile salts produced by the liver and when it is contracted by the entry of food → bile salts travel through the bile duct to the duodenum → causes emulsification of fats, thereby helping in digestion of fat.
  • When the solutes in the gallbladder precipitate, they form gallstones.
  • Patients may have pain from the gallstones, usually after a fatty meal. The pain sites are epigastric or right upper quadrant, which radiates to the right shoulder. Also, cholecystitis and pancreatitis (stones → bile duct -> obstruct biliary flow → jaundice or irritate the pancreas).
  • Obstruction of bile duct → bile salts cannot enter the digestive tract → recycling and excretion of bile salts, digestion of fats and formation of chylomicrons are decreased →  fats in the feces are increased (Steatorrhea).

 

Ref: Harper 30/e: p 255-257, 149-150.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the given diagram:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Liposome

 

Option A:

 

  • Liposomes are microscopic spherical vesicles formed when phospholipids are mixed in water under special conditions, they arrange themselves to form a bilayer membrane which encloses some of the water in a phospholipid sphere.
  • Unilamellar or multilamellar liposomes may be formed.
  • They act as carriers for drugs, proteins, enzymes, genes, etc. which may be encapsulated by the liposomes and taken to target organs.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B: Lipid Bilayer: The self-assembly of phospholipids molecules into monolayers with the polar heads in one direction and the nonpolar tails in the opposite direction to form bilayers. They act as detergents, emulsifying agents, and pulmonary surfactants etc.

 

 

Option C: Micelle: These are molecular aggregates formed when phospholipids are distributed in water and their hydrophobic parts keep away from water and are involved in solubilization of lipids in aqueous media and in digestion and absorption of lipids.

 

Option D: Aquasome: These are nanoparticulate carrier systems with three layered self-assembled structures comprise the central solid nanocrystalline core coated with polyhydroxy oligomers onto which biochemically active molecules are adsorbed. They act as a carrier system for delivery of insulin, haemoglobin and various antigens etc.

 

Educational objective:

 

Liposome, which is a spherical vesicle having at least one lipid bilayer. The liposome can be used to deliver drugs or genetic material into a cell. It is composed of phospholipids that form a bilayer similar to the cell membrane with an aqueous interior; this structure is ideal for encapsulating aqueous solutions of hydrophilic drugs.

pan style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Option A: PUFA is essential for membrane structure: This is true. Polyunsaturated fatty acids are crucial for maintaining the fluidity and functionality of cell membranes.

questions.stem: Following a substantial meal, an individual's metabolic processes adjust to manage the influx of nutrients. In adipocytes, specifically, one enzyme becomes particularly active to facilitate the storage of excess energy. Which enzyme is primarily activated in adipocytes postprandially?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Phosphatidate phosphatase

 

Option D:

 

  • This enzyme converts phosphatidic acid to DAG during synthesis of triacylglycerol (TAG).
  • The function of adipose tissue is the storage of FA’s as TAGs in fed state and the release of fatty acids during times of fasting or starvation.
  • Fatty acids taken in by adipocytes are stored by esterification to glycerol-3-phosphate (derived almost entirely from the glycolytic intermediate DHAP through the action of glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Glycolytic enzymes are active in adipocytes during triglyceride synthesis, but those of glycogen degradation (low levels in adipocytes) and gluconeogenesis (glucose-6-phosphatase) are not.

 

Option B: It is not present much in adipocytes, so that glycerol released during lipolysis is not used to reesterify the fatty acids being freed.


Option C: It is turned on by phosphorylation by a cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase following epinephrine stimulation in fasting state.

 

Educational objective:

 

Phosphatidate phosphatase plays a crucial role in adipocytes following a heavy meal by catalyzing the dephosphorylation of phosphatidic acid to diacylglycerol, which is a key step in the synthesis of triacylglycerol (the storage form of fats).

 

Postprandially, when there is an abundance of dietary fats and carbohydrates, the body prioritizes the storage of excess energy as fat in adipocytes, and phosphatidate phosphatase is instrumental in this process.

 

Ref: Vasudevan 9 /ed: p 160.

questions.stemHtml: A 52-years-old man weighing 90 kg doing sedentary work denies any health issues. Routine blood test results were all normal except for plasma total cholesterol of 288 mg/dl. He was not willing to take treatment for his hypercholesterolemia. So, analysis of his 1-day dietary chart comes as follows: So, which of the following can be decreased from the diet to reduce the high plasma cholesterol levels?

Ans. D) Saturated fat

 

Option D:

 

  • The intake of saturated fat most likely influences plasma cholesterol in the given diet.
  • The patient is consuming a high-calorie, high-fat diet with 35-40% of the fat as saturated fat.
  • The most important dietary recommendations are reducing the total calorie intake, substitute MUFA & PUFA for saturated fats and also increase dietary fibre.
  • Though a decrease in dietary cholesterol can have effects on the lipid profile, it is always a secondary option to saturated fat.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Carbohydrate: It provides almost 60–65% of total calories and dietary fibre, which improves bowel motility, prevents constipation, and decreases the reabsorption of bile acids thereby reducing the cholesterol level and improves glucose tolerance.

 

Option B: Cholesterol: It is always advised to reduce that dietary intake of cholesterol due to its atherogenic effect and the risk of developing coronary artery disease.


Option C: Unsaturated fat: Saturated fats increase the serum cholesterol and unsaturated fats (vegetable oils and fish oils) reduces it. Especially PUFAs causes esterification and excretion of cholesterol, thereby reducing the cholesterol level in blood. Hence they are antiatherogenic and always preferred in the diet.

A reduction in saturated fat intake is often recommended to lower plasma cholesterol levels. Saturated fats can increase low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, which is a major risk factor for coronary artery disease. The patient's diet, with 78g of saturated fat, significantly exceeds the American Heart Association's recommendation of 5-6% of total daily calories from saturated fat.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old obese woman started with Tab. Orlistat, as she fails to follow the lifestyle modifications advised by her physician. Which of the following steps of digestion and absorption of fats is directly inhibited by Orlistat?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Pancreatic and gastric lipase

 

Option C:

 

  • Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases, thus preventing the digestion and absorption of fats.

 

Sequence of events in digestion:

 

  • Triglycerides are emulsified by bile salts → then acted on by lipases.
  • The product of digestion is absorbed → re-esterified/ resynthesis of TAG in the intestinal mucosal cells → TAG is then packed in the chylomicrons → transported to the peripheral cells for utilization.

 

Effect of orlistat:

 

  • Triglycerides are left undigested and unabsorbed → resulting in bulky stools.
  • Orlistat therapy if given for a long time → induce deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Bile salt formation: Bile salts are produced in the liver from cholesterol and play a crucial role in emulsifying fats in the small intestine to aid in their digestion. Orlistat does not directly inhibit bile salt formation; its action is focused on blocking the enzymes that break down fats into absorbable units.

 

Option B: Micelle formation: Micelles are formed in the small intestine and are essential for the absorption of digested fats. They are composed of bile salts, fatty acids, cholesterol, and other lipids. While Orlistat’s action reduces the amount of free fatty acids available for micelle formation (by inhibiting lipase activity), it does not directly inhibit the formation of micelles themselves.

 

Option D: Absorption of Free fatty acids: Orlistat indirectly affects the absorption of free fatty acids by inhibiting their release from dietary fats. However, the drug does not directly inhibit the cellular mechanisms responsible for the absorption of free fatty acids across the intestinal lining.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The key takeaway is that Orlistat specifically inhibits the action of pancreatic and gastric lipases, enzymes critical for the breakdown of dietary fats into smaller, absorbable molecules like free fatty acids and monoglycerides. By doing so, it reduces the overall absorption of fats from the diet, aiding in weight management. It does not directly affect bile salt formation, micelle formation, or the absorption mechanism of free fatty acids.

 

Ref: Lippincott 6/e: p 175-177.



Lippincott 6/e: p 175-177.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the precursors used in the synthesis of carotenoids?
questions.solutionHtml:
Option A: Amino acids are not directly involved in the synthesis of carotenoids. While amino acids are crucial for protein synthesis and other metabolic functions, they do not serve as precursors for carotenoid synthesis.

 

Option C: Fatty acids are involved in various metabolic processes, including energy storage and membrane synthesis, but they are not directly converted into carotenoids. The elongation of fatty acids refers to the process of adding carbon units to a fatty acid chain, not the synthesis of carotenoids.

 

Option D: Glucose is a central molecule in energy metabolism, participating in pathways such as glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. However, glucose is not directly used in the synthesis of carotenoids. While some of the intermediates from glucose metabolism might contribute to the pool of precursors for isoprene unit synthesis, glucose itself is not a direct precursor for carotenoids.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Isoprene units are precursors to many Isoprenoid compounds such as

 

  • Vitamin A
  • Vitamin K

questions.stem: A 75-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease (CAD), who recently underwent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), is scheduled for a postoperative follow-up visit. During the visit, the cardiologist reviews the patient's postoperative recovery and emphasizes the importance of dietary and lifestyle modifications to manage his CAD and reduce the risk of future cardiac events. The cardiologist outlines several recommendations but also wants to clarify a common misconception about dietary guidelines for patients with a high risk of coronary heart disease. Which of the following dietary goals is NOT typically recommended for patients with a high risk of coronary heart disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
> dietary patterns and saturated fat intake.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: LDL cholesterol < 100 mg/dl: This target is recommended for individuals with CAD to reduce the risk of further coronary events. Lowering LDL cholesterol is a key focus in managing CAD because elevated LDL levels are directly linked to an increased risk of atherosclerosis and subsequent heart problems.

 

Option B: Saturated fat <7% of total calories: Reducing saturated fat intake is crucial for individuals with CAD as saturated fats can raise LDL cholesterol levels, contributing to the buildup of plaques in arteries. Limiting saturated fats to less than 7% of total daily calories is part of a heart-healthy diet aimed at reducing cardiovascular risk.

 

Option D: Avoid Alcohol: Moderation in alcohol consumption is generally advised for the general population. For patients with CAD, alcohol should be consumed with caution due to its potential effects on blood pressure, triglyceride levels, and caloric intake. While moderate alcohol intake may have some cardiovascular benefits in certain individuals, avoiding excessive alcohol is crucial, especially for those with CAD or those who have difficulty consuming alcohol in moderation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • For managing coronary artery disease, dietary recommendations emphasize reducing saturated fat intake and maintaining LDL cholesterol levels below 100 mg/dl. The strict limit on dietary cholesterol (<300 mg/day) is less emphasized, while moderation in alcohol consumption is advised for overall heart health.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Crystalline cholesterol monohydrate                         

 

Option B:

 

  • Components: cholesterol monohydrate crystals, calcium bilirubinate, and bile salts.
  • Small changes in the composition of bile can result in crystallization of cholesterol as gallstones and it is also formed when the solutes in the gallbladder precipitate
  • Cholesterol stones (80% of gallstones) are usually yellow-green in appearance
  • C/F: pain (epigastric or right upper quadrant and radiating to the right shoulder) from the gallstones, usually after a fatty meal.

Other Options:

questions.stem: Secondary bile acids are:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid

 

Option C:

 

Secondary bile acids, which include deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid, are formed by the bacterial action on primary bile acids in the intestine. Primary bile acids, such as cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid, are synthesized in the liver. When they are secreted into the intestine, gut bacteria can modify them to form secondary bile acids.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid: These are primary bile acids synthesized in the liver from cholesterol.

 

Option B: Cholic acid and deoxycholic acid: Cholic acid is a primary bile acid, whereas deoxycholic acid is a secondary bile acid.

 

Option D: Lithocholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid: Lithocholic acid is a secondary bile acid, while chenodeoxycholic acid is a primary bile acid.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Primary Bile Acids: Formed in Liver

 

  1. Cholic Acid (Most abundant bile acids in mammals)
  2. Chenodeoxycholic Acid

 

Secondary Bile acids: Formed in Intestine

 

  1. Deoxycholic Acid
  2. Lithocholic Acid

questions.stem: Bile acids are primarily synthesized from which of the following substances?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cholesterol

 

Option A:

 

Bile acids are synthesized from cholesterol in the liver. This process involves multiple enzymatic steps that convert cholesterol into primary bile acids, such as cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid. These bile acids play a critical role in the digestion and absorption of dietary fats and fat-soluble vitamins in the intestine.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B: Fatty acid: Fatty acids are key components of fats and are involved in various metabolic processes, but they are not the precursors for bile acid synthesis.

 

Option C: Bilirubin: Bilirubin is a breakdown product of heme from hemoglobin in red blood cells. It is excreted in bile but is not a precursor to bile acid synthesis.

 

Option D: Proteins: Proteins serve numerous functions in the body, including acting as enzymes and structural components, but they are not directly involved in the synthesis of bile acids.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Bile acids are synthesized from cholesterol in liver.
  • Rate limiting enzyme: seven α hydroxylase, Microsomal enzyme: Cyt P450, O2, NADPH, Vit C.

Explanation:

 

Assertion (A) is wrong because Metachromatic Leukodystrophy (MLD) is not a glycogen storage disease. It is a lysosomal storage disorder that belongs to the group of sphingolipidoses, caused by a deficiency in the enzyme arylsulfatase A. This leads to the accumulation of sulfatides, particularly sulfogalactocerebroside, resulting in demyelination of white matter, particularly in the central and peripheral nervous systems.

 

Clinical features of MLD include:

  • Progressive neurological deterioration
  • Behavioral changes, motor regression
  • Demyelination, often leading to spasticity and paralysis

 

Reason (R) is also wrong because hexosaminidase A deficiency is the cause of Tay-Sachs disease, not MLD.

  • Tay-Sachs is another lysosomal storage disorder, characterized by accumulation of GM2 gangliosides due to hexosaminidase A deficiency.
  • It presents with progressive neurodegeneration, cherry-red spot in macula, and no hepatosplenomegaly.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • MLD: Caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency, leading to sulfatide accumulation, affects myelin, results in leukodystrophy.
  • Tay-Sachs: Caused by hexosaminidase A deficiency, results in ganglioside accumulation, primarily a neurodegenerative condition without organ enlargement.

In Niemann-Pick disease type A and B, there is an accumulation of sphingomyelin due to a deficiency in the enzyme sphingomyelinase. questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old man presents to the emergency department with an episode of sudden rectal hemorrhage. His medical history is non-specific, but on examination, he is found to have hepatosplenomegaly. A complete blood count reveals thrombocytopenia, and a liver biopsy shows abnormal cells within Glisson's capsule. Given these findings, the medical team suspects a lysosomal storage disorder and further diagnostic tests are conducted. Which of the following metabolic disorders is the patient least likely to have, given the clinical findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
p>Explanation:

 

Tay-Sachs disease is the least likely diagnosis in this clinical scenario. It is a lysosomal storage disorder, its classic features include:

  • Neurodegeneration
  • Cherry-red spot on the macula
  • Developmental regression
  • No hepatosplenomegaly
  • No thrombocytopenia

 

In contrast, this patient has hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and abnormal liver histology, which are not characteristic of Tay-Sachs.

 

Other Options:

  • Option A. Gaucher’s disease:
    • Consistent with hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia
    • Presence of Gaucher cells (lipid-laden macrophages) in liver biopsy
    • Neurological symptoms are absent in Type 1 (non-neuronopathic form), which can occur in adults
  • Option B. Niemann-Pick disease:
    • Can show cherry-red spots, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurologic signs
    • Liver involvement is common
  • Option D. Sandhoff’s disease:
    • Similar to Tay-Sachs but with systemic features including hepatosplenomegaly
    • Cherry-red spot may be seen

 

Educational Objective:

 

Differentiate lysosomal storage disorders based on systemic vs. neurological findings:

  • Tay-Sachs: Purely neurological, no organomegaly, presents in infancy
  • Gaucher’s disease: Can present with hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and bone involvement, especially in Type 1

Niemann-Pick and Sandhoff: Share both visceral and neurological features including cherry-red spots

questions.stem: A teenage boy, self-conscious about his weight, decides to follow a fat-free diet in hopes of improving his physique. After adhering to this dietary regimen for several weeks, he visits a nutritionist for a consultation. Concerned about potential nutritional deficiencies and their impact on lipid metabolism, the nutritionist reviews the boy's diet and decides to assess his body's ability to synthesize various essential lipids that might be affected by his restrictive diet:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Prostaglandins

 

Option B:

 

Prostaglandins are synthesized from essential fatty acids, such as arachidonic acid, which are typically obtained from dietary fats. A fat-free diet could lead to a deficiency in essential fatty acids, impacting the body's ability to synthesize prostaglandins. Prostaglandins play various roles in the body, including inflammation, pain modulation, and regulation of blood flow.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Cholesterol: The body can synthesize cholesterol endogenously, primarily in the liver, and its synthesis is less likely to be directly affected by a fat-free diet.

 

Option C: Glycolipids: Glycolipids are composed of a carbohydrate and a lipid. While dietary fats influence lipid components, the body can also synthesize these from other sources.

 

Option D: Phospholipids: Phospholipids can be synthesized endogenously from glycerol, fatty acids, and phosphate. The body can adapt to variations in dietary fat intake to maintain phospholipid synthesis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Prostaglandins are synthesized from arachidonic acid.

  • Arachidonic acid is synthesized from linoleic acid, which is an essential fatty acid supplied from dietary lipids in adequate amounts.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with a family history of ischemic heart disease (IHD) presents to the emergency room with chest pain. After thorough evaluation, including blood tests and ECG, which were found to be normal, she is kept under observation due to her risk factors. Considering her family history and presenting symptoms, the attending physician decides to initiate a preventive treatment regimen. She is prescribed a low dose of Aspirin, a well-known cardio-protective medication, which acts by inhibiting the cyclooxygenase (COX) enzyme. The physician explains the importance of COX in the synthesis of certain molecules from arachidonic acid and how Aspirin's action helps in her condition:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Thromboxane from arachidonic acid

 

Option A:

 

  • Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclo-oxygenase-1 of platelets and inhibits the enzyme →Thromboxane (TxA2) is not formed →no vasoconstriction and no platelet aggregation →Prevent thrombus formation.

 

 

  • Aspirin also inhibits production of Prostacyclin (PGI2) by endothelial cells → prevents platelet aggregation → produces vasodilatation.
  • But unlike platelets, the endothelial cells regenerate cyclooxygenase within a few hours.
  • Aspirin is clinically used for prevention and management of Angina, myocardial infarction, stroke, and Transient Ischaemic attacks (TIA).              

 

Other Options:

 

Option B: Leukotrienes from Arachidonic acid: These are formed from lipo-oxygenase pathway.

 

Option C: Phospholipids from Arachidonic acid: PGs are stored in membranes as phospholipids and arachidonic acid is released by the action of phospholipase A2 on phospholipids.

 

Option D: Arachidonic acid from Linoleic acid: Linoleic acid can be converted to arachidonic acid by elongation and desaturation (with the help of desaturase and elongase) and if the dietary supply of linoleic acid is sufficient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Aspirin’s cardio-protective effect is attributed to its ability to inhibit the COX enzyme, thereby decreasing the production of thromboxane A2 from arachidonic acid. This action reduces platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, lowering the risk of thrombotic events in patients with a high risk of ischemic heart disease.

 

Ref: Harper 30/e:  p 239-240, 720.




Harper 30/e: p 239-240, 720.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with coronary artery disease (CAD) is being successfully treated with anti-atherogenic medication that targets PCSK9. Following treatment, his lipid profile normalizes, and his cardiac status improves. What is the primary function of PCSK9?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibiting the binding of apoB to LDL receptor, thereby blocking the lipoprotein uptake and increasing the blood cholesterol levels

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Decreasing the availability of LDL receptors on the cell surface, resulting in decreased LDL uptake and high blood cholesterol level
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Decreasing the availability of LDL receptors on the cell surface, resulting in decreased LDL uptake and high blood cholesterol level

 

PCSK9 (Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin Type 9) normally binds to LDL receptors and promotes their degradation in lysosomes, which prevents the receptors from being recycled back to the cell surface. This natural function of PCSK9 decreases the number of LDL receptors available on cell surfaces, especially hepatocytes, resulting in reduced LDL clearance from the bloodstream and consequently higher blood cholesterol levels.

 

Anti-atherogenic medications that target PCSK9 (PCSK9 inhibitors) work by inhibiting this protein, thereby preventing LDL receptor degradation. This leads to:

  • Increased recycling of LDL receptors back to the cell surface
  • Greater availability of LDL receptors on hepatocytes
  • Enhanced clearance of LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream
  • Reduced blood LDL cholesterol levels
  • Improved cardiovascular outcomes

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Increasing the synthesis and secretion of VLDL - PCSK9 does not directly affect VLDL synthesis or secretion; its primary role is related to LDL receptor regulation.

 

Option B: Inhibiting the binding of apoB to the LDL receptor - PCSK9 does not interfere with apoB binding to LDL receptors; it affects the degradation of LDL receptors themselves.

 

Option D: Preventing the breakdown of cholesterol into bile acids - PCSK9's function is not related to cholesterol metabolism into bile acids; it specifically impacts the recycling and degradation of LDL receptors.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Understanding that PCSK9 inhibitors work by preventing PCSK9-mediated degradation of LDL receptors, thereby increasing LDL receptor availability, enhancing LDL cholesterol clearance, and lowering blood cholesterol levels in patients with coronary artery disease.

questions.stemHtml: In an electrophoretic separation procedure, a technician observes the migration of lipoproteins from the cathode (-) to the anode (+) sidewhich of the following correctly orders the lipoproteins from cathode to anode?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) CM > LDL > VLDL > HDL

 

Option A:

 

Plasma lipoproteins can be separated on the basis of their electrophoretic mobility:

Those with higher protein content will move faster towards the anode and those with less proteins have low mobility

 

Classifcation of Lipoproteins

 

Depending on the density (by ultracentrifugation) or on the electrophoretic mobility, the lipoproteins in plasma are classified into five major types 

  1. Chylomicrons: Contain apoprotein B-48.
  2. Very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) or pre-beta lipoproteins. Main apoprotein is B-100.
  3. Intermediate density lipoproteins (IDL) or broad-beta lipoproteins
  4. Low-density lipoproteins or beta lipoproteins. Major apoprotein in LDL is B-100.
  5. High-density lipoproteins or alpha lipoproteins. Major apoprotein in HDL is apo A.

 

Separation by Ultracentrifugation

The lipoproteins are characterized on the basis of their density. Fat is less dense than water; so fat floats on water. Lipoproteins with high lipid content will have a low density and so float on centrifugation. Those with high protein content will sediment easily and have a high density. 

 

Separation by Electrophoresis

As a general rule, those with higher protein content will move faster towards the anode and those with fewer proteins have minimum mobility.

 

Note : pattern of electrophoresis and ultracentrifugation are different as shown in the diagram.

 

Electrophoresis 

 

Standard order from Cathode (-) to Anode (+):

CM >LDL>VLDL>HDL 

 

Ultracentrifugation: sequence is 

CM > VLDL > LDL > HDL

 

 

Comparison of electrophoretic and ultracentrifugation patterns of lipoproteins.

(VLDL: very low-density lipoproteins; IDL: intermediate density lipoproteins; LDL: low-density lipoproteins; HDL: high-density lipoproteins; FFA: free fatty acid)

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lipoprotein electrophoresis separates particles based on their protein content and charge. Understanding the typical migration pattern helps diagnose dyslipidemias and distinguish between different lipoprotein abnormalities.

On examination, he exhibits skin findings as shown in the image, with a blood sample that appears creamy and shows elevated triglycerides levels. sp;

Explanation:

 

Familial Hyper Chylomicronemia Syndrome (also known as Type I Hyperlipoproteinemia) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency or dysfunction, or by apo C-II deficiency, which is a necessary cofactor for LPL activation.

 

Key clinical features:

  • Eruptive xanthomas (small, yellow papules, especially on the buttocks or extensor surfaces)
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Recurrent abdominal pain (may be related to pancreatitis)
  • Milky or creamy plasma appearance
  • Very high serum triglyceride levels, often >1000 mg/dL

Although this condition typically presents in childhood or adolescence, adult presentations can occur, especially if the diagnosis is delayed or partial enzyme activity exists.

 

Other Options:

 

  • Option A: Broad Beta Disease (Type III Hyperlipoproteinemia) – Associated with palmar xanthomas and elevated remnants. Presents with increased cardiovascular risk.
  • Option B: Abetalipoproteinemia – Features very low serum triglycerides and cholesterol, acanthocytosis, fat malabsorption, and retinal degeneration. Plasma is not creamy.
  • Option D: Familial Hypercholesterolemia (Type IIa) – Caused by LDL receptor mutations, presents with tendinous xanthomas, corneal arcus, and very high LDL cholesterol levels. Triglycerides are usually normal.

 

Educational Objective:


Recognize Familial Chylomicronemia Syndrome by:

  • Eruptive xanthomas
  • Creamy plasma with markedly elevated triglycerides

It reflects a defect in chylomicron clearance, due to LPL enzyme deficiency or its apo C-II cofactor, resulting in accumulation of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins in plasma.

For optimal cardiovascular health, particularly in primary prevention (patients without existing cardiovascular disease), the recommended upper limit for LDL cholesterol is typically ≤100 mg/dL.

questions.stem: A research team studying metabolic responses to nutrient deprivation measures enzymatic activities in subjects after a 24-hour fast. They aim to determine which enzyme associated with lipid metabolism shows decreased activity in this energy-conserving state. Which enzyme is the research team least likely to find elevated in the fasting state?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Acetyl CoA carboxylase

 

Option D:

 

  • Phosphorylation inactivates acetyl CoA carboxylase. Thus, AMP activated kinase (AMPK) phosphorylates acetyl CoA carboxylase and inactivates it
  • ATP inhibits AMPK, hence fatty acid synthesis is increased in a well-fed state.
  • Fatty acid synthesis decreases in fasting state
  • This enzyme is inhibited by palmitoyl CoA, the end product of fatty acid synthesis
  • Dephosphorylation of Acetyl CoA carboxylase is effected by protein phosphatase 1.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: CPS–I: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is an enzyme in the urea cycle, which may have increased activity during fasting due to the breakdown of amino acids for gluconeogenesis, resulting in excess nitrogen that needs to be excreted as urea.

 

Option B: Hormone-sensitive lipase: This enzyme is responsible for breaking down stored triglycerides in adipose tissue into free fatty acids and glycerol, which is upregulated during fasting to provide energy.

 

Option C: Glycogen Phosphorylase: This enzyme breaks down glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate, which is then converted to glucose-6-phosphate for gluconeogenesis or energy production, and is thus upregulated during fasting.

 

Educational Objective:

 

During fasting, the body downregulates enzymes involved in synthesizing storage compounds, such as acetyl CoA carboxylase, while upregulating enzymes that facilitate the mobilization of stored nutrients, like hormone-sensitive lipase and glycogen phosphorylase.

questions.stem: Identify the metabolic pathway that specifically utilizes NADPH as a reducing agent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Fatty acid synthesis

 

Option A:

 

NADPH provides the reducing equivalents necessary for the biosynthesis of fatty acids. It is used in the reductive reactions of the fatty acid synthesis pathway, such as the conversion of acetoacetyl-ACP to malonyl-ACP, and is a critical factor in the synthesis of new fatty acid molecules.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B: Ketone synthesis: This process takes place predominantly in the mitochondria of liver cells during periods of carbohydrate scarcity and does not primarily use NADPH.

 

Option C: Gluconeogenesis: This is the pathway by which glucose is synthesized from non-carbohydrate precursors, and it does not typically involve NADPH.

 

Option D: Glycolysis: This is the metabolic pathway that breaks down glucose to pyruvate, generating ATP and NADH, not utilizing NADPH.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Fatty acid synthesis require Cofactors like: NADPH, ATP, Mn2+ , HCO3- , Biotin

questions.stem: Identify which of the following is not utilized in the synthesis of fatty acids:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) FADH2

 

Option C:

 

FADH2 is a reduced form of flavin adenine dinucleotide that is primarily involved as an electron carrier in the mitochondrial electron transport chain to produce ATP. It is not used as a direct substrate or cofactor in the biosynthetic pathway of fatty acids.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: ATP: ATP provides the energy necessary for the activation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA in the first step of fatty acid synthesis.

 

Option B: NADPH: NADPH is a reducing agent that donates electrons in the reductive biosynthetic steps of fatty acid synthesis.

 

Option D: HCO3- (bicarbonate): Bicarbonate serves as a source of the carboxyl group in the conversion of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase during fatty acid synthesis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Two major enzyme complexes are involved in the synthesis of fatty acids.
  • The first is acetyl-CoA carboxylase, which synthesizes malonyl-CoA by  the  steps shown below for the synthesis of palmitate:
  • 7 acetyl-CoA + 7 HCO3- + 7 ATP → 7 malonyl-CoA + 7 ADP + 7 Pi
  • Using the malonyl-CoA, palmitate is then synthesized by seven cycles of the fatty acid synthetase complex, whose stoichiometry is summarized below:
  • acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA + 14 NADPH → palmitate + 7 CO2 +14 NAD+ + 8 CoA + 6 H2O
  • As can be seen from the equations above, the necessary amount of malonyl-CoA is synthesized. Palmitate is subsequently synthesized from malonyl-CoA and one initial acetyl-CoA. Thus, acetyl-CoA, NADPH, ATP, and HCO3- are all necessary in this process.

The endoplasmic reticulum is the key organelle involved in the elongation of long-chain fatty acids. This process is crucial for the synthesis of various complex lipids that are integral to cellular membranes and signaling pathways.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B: Golgi body: The Golgi apparatus is primarily involved in the modification, sorting, and packaging of proteins and lipids for secretion or use within the cell. It is not directly involved in the elongation of fatty acids.

 

Option C: Lysosomes: Lysosomes are organelles that contain digestive enzymes used for breaking down various biomolecules, cellular debris, and foreign pathogens. They are not involved in the synthesis or elongation of fatty acids.

 

Option D: Ribosomes: Ribosomes are the cellular structures responsible for protein synthesis, translating mRNA into polypeptide chains. They do not participate in fatty acid elongation or lipid metabolism directly.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The Microsomal system (microsomal fatty acid elongase system) elongates saturated or unsaturated fatty acyl CoA by addition of two-carbon units successively.
  • Donor of 2 carbon acetyl groups: Malonyl CoA.
  • NADPH is needed for the reaction.
  • This system can elongate FA having 10C units onwards up to the length of 22 or 24C.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has been observing a fast as part of a cultural festival for several days. Despite significantly reduced food intake, he surprisingly reports feeling mentally alert and does not experience any dizziness or significant discomfort typically associated with low blood sugar levels. Intrigued by this adaptation, he visits a healthcare provider for a routine check-up. The provider explains how the body adapts to prolonged fasting by utilizing alternative energy sources to maintain brain function and overall metabolism:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Beta-hydroxybutyrate.

 

Option C:

 

  • Ketone bodies include acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone, which are produced by the liver in the fasting state by beta-oxidation of fatty acids. 
  • Then these ketone bodies are released into the bloodstream →used as alternative energy sources for muscle, kidney, and brain. 
  • But the brain specifically requires a small amount of circulating glucose to function and the amount required is reduced when ketone body sources are available.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Coenzyme A: It is found in mitochondria and carries acetyl groups into the TCA cycle.

 

Option B: Beta-carotene: It is a vitamin with antioxidant properties.

 

Option D: Apoprotein: It is one of the proteins that hold lipoproteins together.

 

Educational Objective:

 

During prolonged fasting, the body shifts to ketosis, a metabolic state where it uses ketone bodies as an alternative energy source. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is one of the primary ketone bodies produced by the liver from fatty acids in the absence of sufficient glucose. The brain can utilize beta-hydroxybutyrate efficiently in place of glucose, allowing for sustained cognitive function and energy levels despite low blood glucose.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with severe polyuria and polydipsia. Laboratory tests reveal the presence of ketones in her urine. Considering the metabolic conditions, which is the most likely source of these ketones?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Free fatty acid breakdown      

 

 Option B:

                   

  • The presenting features are suggestive of type 1 diabetes. 
  • The primary source of ketones is free fatty acid breakdown. 
  • Ketone body formation occurs as follows: Insulin deficiency → activated lipolysis → increased plasma free fatty acids  → increased hepatic fatty acids → accelerated ketogenesis → ketosis

 

other options:

 

Option A. Gluconeogenesis: While gluconeogenesis involves the production of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, it does not directly lead to ketone production. It is a glucose-generating process that occurs in the liver and kidneys.

 

Option C. Glycogenolysis: This process involves the breakdown of glycogen stored in the liver and muscle into glucose. Glycogenolysis does not directly result in ketone production; instead, it provides an immediate source of glucose.

 

Option D. Triglyceride breakdown: Triglyceride breakdown in adipose tissue leads to the release of glycerol and free fatty acids. While the breakdown of triglycerides initiates the release of fatty acids, it is the subsequent β-oxidation of these fatty acids in the liver that leads directly to ketone production. Therefore, "free fatty acid breakdown" is a more specific answer in the context of ketone production.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ketone bodies are produced primarily in the liver through the process of ketogenesis, which occurs when there is an increased breakdown of free fatty acids. This situation typically arises in states of decreased carbohydrate availability or impaired glucose utilization, leading the body to switch to fat as an alternative energy source. In this patient's case, the presence of ketones in the urine suggests that her body is utilizing fatty acids for energy, which results in the production of ketones as a byproduct of fatty acid metabolism in the liver.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman embarks on a ketogenic diet as part of a weight loss plan. After a few weeks, she notices some symptoms and decides to consult her family physician. The healthcare provider explains the physiological state her body is in due to the high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet and discusses the signs and implications of this metabolic state:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) All the above

 

Option D:

 

  • Normally the rate of synthesis of ketone bodies by the liver is well balanced by their metabolism by extrahepatic tissues → causes blood level of ketone bodies << 1 mg/dL and only traces are excreted in urine.

 

 

  • When the rate of synthesis exceeds the ability of utilization → accumulation of ketone bodies in blood (Ketonemia), excretion in urine (ketonuria) and smell of acetone in breath.
  • All these three constitute together to form ketosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Ketonemia: This term refers to the presence of ketone bodies in the blood. It is one of the hallmark signs of ketosis, indicating that the body is using ketones as an alternative energy source due to low glucose availability or utilization.

 

Option B: Ketonuria: Ketonuria denotes the excretion of ketone bodies in the urine. It's a direct result of ketonemia; when ketone levels in the blood rise, the kidneys filter some of these ketones out, which then appear in the urine. It's often used as a diagnostic indicator for ketosis.

 

Option C: Smell of acetone: Acetone, one of the three primary ketone bodies (alongside acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate), can be exhaled in the breath when in ketosis, leading to a distinct fruity or nail polish remover-like smell. This is a common anecdotal marker of being in a state of ketosis, especially noted among individuals following a ketogenic diet.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ketosis is characterized by elevated levels of ketone bodies, which can manifest as ketonemia (presence of ketones in the blood), ketonuria (presence of ketones in the urine), and a distinctive acetone smell in the breath. Understanding these manifestations provides insights into the body's metabolic state during carbohydrate restriction, fasting, or uncontrolled diabetes, highlighting the body's adaptive mechanisms to alternative energy sources.

questions.stem: Which of the following is unable to utilize ketone bodies as an energy source?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) RBCs

 

Option C:

 

Red blood cells (RBCs) are unable to utilize ketone bodies due to the absence of mitochondria, where ketone bodies are converted into acetyl-CoA and then enter the citric acid cycle for energy production. RBCs rely solely on glycolysis for their energy needs.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Brain: The brain can utilize ketone bodies as an alternative energy source during prolonged fasting or carbohydrate restriction, after an adaptation period.

 

Option B: Skeletal muscle: Skeletal muscles can use ketone bodies for energy, especially during prolonged periods of fasting or intense exercise when glucose availability is limited.

 

Option D: Cardiac muscle: The heart can efficiently use ketone bodies as a fuel source, particularly in conditions where fatty acid oxidation is compromised or in the context of increased energy demand.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The ketone bodies are formed in the liver by mitochondrial enzyme thiolase and are utilized by extrahepatic tissues such as heart muscle, renal cortex, skeletal muscle, and brain, which prefer the ketone bodies as alternate sources of energy, if glucose is not available.
  • Ketone bodies are not utilised by RBCs due to the absence of mitochondria

questions.stem: Which enzyme is common to the synthesis pathways of both ketone bodies and cholesterol?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) HMG CoA Synthase

 

Option A:

 

HMG CoA Synthase is the enzyme involved in the synthesis of both ketone bodies and cholesterol. It catalyzes the condensation of acetoacetyl-CoA with another molecule of acetyl-CoA to form 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA), which is a crucial step in both pathways. In the liver, the presence of HMG CoA Synthase in the mitochondria facilitates the production of ketone bodies, whereas in the cytoplasm, it participates in the early steps of cholesterol biosynthesis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B: HMG CoA Lyase is involved in the ketogenesis pathway, specifically in the breakdown of HMG-CoA to acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA, but it does not play a role in cholesterol synthesis.

 

Option C: HMG CoA Reductase is a key enzyme in the cholesterol synthesis pathway, catalyzing the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate. This enzyme is the target of statin drugs, which are used to lower cholesterol levels.

 

Option D: HMG CoA Carboxylase is involved in fatty acid synthesis, converting acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, and is not directly involved in the synthesis of ketone bodies or cholesterol.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Acetyl CoA combines with acetoacetyl CoA → HMG CoA by the enzyme HMG CoA synthase.
  • Mitochondrial HMG CoA is used for ketogenesis, and cytosolic fraction is used for cholesterol synthesis.

questions.stem: In a pediatric clinic, a physician evaluates a 7-month-old male infant presented by his mother with concerns about hypotonia, hepatomegaly, and delayed developmental milestones. Suspecting Zellweger syndrome, a peroxisomal disorder, the physician considers the metabolic abnormalities associated with this condition. Which type of fatty acids is known to accumulate in patients with Zellweger syndrome?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Very long chain fatty acids                                   

 

Option D:

 

  • Zellweger syndrome is also known as Cerebrohepatorenal syndrome which is due to defective oxidation of very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA).
  • Due to mutations in peroxins genes , entry of enzymes into the peroxisomes are denied causing insufficient oxidation of VLCFA leading to its accumulation in CNS causing neurological impairment and death in childhood.
  • It usually presents at birth with profound neurologic impairment and the victims often dying within a year.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: They do not require carnitine for transport across the inner mitochondrial membrane and so are easily oxidized.

 

Option B: Long chain fatty acid accumulation is due to deficiency of long chain acyl CoA dehydrogenase resulting in Nonketotic hypoglycaemia with low carnitine and increased acyl carnitine in plasma.

 

Option C: MCAD accumulation occurs due to deficiency of medium chain acyl CoA dehydrogenase results in acidosis, hyperammonemia, hypoglycaemia and fatty liver.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Zellweger syndrome is a peroxisomal disorder characterized by the absence or malfunction of peroxisomes in the cells. One of the key functions of peroxisomes is the β-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). In Zellweger syndrome, the inability to metabolize VLCFAs leads to their accumulation in tissues and blood, contributing to the clinical manifestations of the disorder.

questions.stemHtml: Based on the diagram provided, which enzyme is not involved in shuttling fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation?

span>

 

Explanation:

 

The diagram shows the carnitine shuttle system, which is responsible for transporting long-chain fatty acids from the cytosol into the mitochondrial matrix, where β-oxidation occurs.

 

Option B. Acyl Co-A Dehydrogenase

  • Location: Mitochondrial matrix
  • Function: Catalyzes the first step of β-oxidation, dehydrogenating Acyl-CoA to form a trans double bond between the α and β carbons.
  • Involved in shuttle?  No – it acts after the fatty acid has already entered the matrix.

 

 

Other Options

 

Option A. Carnitine Palmitoyl Transferase I (CPT I)

  • Location: Outer mitochondrial membrane
  • Function: Converts Acyl-CoA to Acyl-carnitine by transferring the fatty acid to carnitine.
  • Involved in shuttle? Yes

 

Option C. Carnitine Palmitoyl Transferase II (CPT II)

  • Location: Inner mitochondrial membrane (matrix side)
  • Function: Converts Acyl-carnitine back to Acyl-CoA and carnitine, allowing the fatty acid to enter β-oxidation.
  • Involved in shuttle? Yes

 

Option D. Carnitine Acylcarnitine Translocase

  • Location: Inner mitochondrial membrane
  • Function: Transports Acyl-carnitine into the mitochondrial matrix while moving free carnitine back to the cytosol in a counter-transport manner.
  • Involved in shuttle? Yes

 

 

Role of carnitine in the transport of long-chain fatty acids through the inner mitochondrial membrane.


Long-chain acyl-CoA formed by acyl-CoA synthetase enters the intermembrane space. For transport across the inner membrane, acyl groups must be transferred from CoA to carnitine by carnitine palmitoyl transferase-I. The acylcarnitine formed is then carried into the matrix by a translocase enzyme in exchange for a free carnitine and acyl-CoA is reformed by carnitine palmitoyltransferase-II.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Understand the carnitine shuttle system, which is essential for the mitochondrial import of long-chain fatty acids. Key enzymes involved include CPT I, CPT II, and the translocase. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is not involved in transport—it functions after the fatty acid enters the matrix, initiating β-oxidation.

questions.stem: A pediatrician is evaluating a 7-month-old boy who was admitted with a seizure, gastrointestinal symptoms, and decreased appetite. Laboratory tests show severe hypoglycemia, normal blood carnitine levels, absence of ketones in the urine, and the presence of various dicarboxylic acids. These findings suggest a diagnosis of medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency. Considering the biochemistry of MCAD deficiency, what is the underlying cause of fasting hypoglycemia in this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased ability to convert acetyl coenzyme A to glucose

options.label: C
options.text: Increased conversion of acetyl coenzyme A to acetoacetate

options.label: D
options.text: Increased production of ATP and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Decreased acetyl CoA production

 

Option B:

 

MCAD deficiency impairs the body's ability to break down medium-chain fatty acids due to a lack of functional MCAD enzyme. This impedes the production of acetyl CoA from these fatty acids during fasting, when the body normally relies on fat oxidation for energy. Acetyl CoA is crucial for maintaining blood glucose levels via gluconeogenesis during periods without food. In MCAD deficiency, the reduced availability of acetyl CoA limits gluconeogenesis, leading to fasting hypoglycemia

 

 Other Options:

 

Option A: Decreased ability to convert acetyl coenzyme A to glucose: Acetyl CoA cannot be converted to glucose in humans due to the irreversibility of the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction, which is not specific to MCAD deficiency.

 

Option C: Increased conversion of acetyl coenzyme A to acetoacetate: MCAD deficiency would actually lead to a decreased production of ketone bodies like acetoacetate because there is less acetyl CoA available from fatty acid oxidation.

 

Option D: Increased production of ATP and NAD: MCAD deficiency would result in decreased production of ATP and NADH from medium-chain fatty acid oxidation because the fatty acids are not being properly metabolized.

 

Educational Objective:

 

MCAD deficiency leads to decreased acetyl CoA production from medium-chain fatty acids, which impairs gluconeogenesis and energy production during fasting, resulting in hypoglycemia. The disease also leads to an accumulation of fatty acid metabolites, such as dicarboxylic acids, in the blood and urine.

questions.stemHtml: A neonate in the NICU presents with seizures, poor muscle tone, feeding difficulties, distinct facial features, bilateral cataracts, and ultrasound findings of renal cysts. Blood work indicates elevated very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), reduced levels of plasmalogen, and increased levels of cholestenoic acid. Based on these clinical findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Zellweger syndrome

 

Option A:

 

  • Zellweger syndrome is due to defective oxidation of very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA).
  • Peroxisomes are empty or peroxisomal enzymes are not transported correctly into peroxisomes → leads to insufficient oxidation of VLCFA → accumulation of VLCFA in CNS → neurological impairment and death in childhood.
  • Zellweger syndrome, adrenoleukodystrophy and infantile Refsum’s disease are together classified as Peroxisomal biogenesis disorders.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Infantile Refsum's Disease:  It is also a peroxisomal disorder → phytanic acid accumulation along with VLCFA & Children do not survive long.

 

Option  C. Refsum's Disease: Due to lack of alpha-hydroxylase → alpha oxidation does not occur → phytanic acid accumulates in the tissues → C/F: severe neurological symptoms, polyneuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, nerve deafness and cerebellar ataxia.

 

Option D. Organic Acidurias: Disorders of metabolism of fatty acids, branched Chain, aromatic amino acids and citric acid cycle → accumulation of organic acids in body tissues and their excretion in urine → acidosis, vomiting, convulsions and coma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Zellweger syndrome, a peroxisomal biogenesis disorder, is characterized by the absence of functional peroxisomes, which leads to the accumulation of VLCFAs and defects in plasmalogen synthesis necessary for normal cell membrane function.

 

The clinical presentation, including distinctive facial features, cataracts, and renal cysts, along with the specific biochemical abnormalities, strongly suggests Zellweger syndrome.

questions.stemHtml: Review the diagram of the cholesterol molecule, as shown in the image and identify incorrect statements about its structure:

options.label: A
options.text: They have cyclopentano perhydro phenanthrene ring system

options.label: B
options.text: It is made up of 3 cyclohexane rings - A, B and C

options.label: C
options.text: An 8-carbon side chain attached to 17th carbon is characteristic of all sterols

options.label: D
options.text: The OH group is beta oriented

questions.answerText: An 8-carbon side chain attached to 17th carbon is characteristic of all sterols
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) An 8-carbon side chain attached to 17th carbon is characteristic of all sterols

 

Option C:


Option C is incorrect because not all sterols have an 8-carbon side chain at the 17th carbon. While cholesterol specifically has an 8-carbon side chain attached to C-17, other sterols (e.g., plant sterols or bile acids) have variations in side chain length or structure. Therefore, this side chain is not a universal feature of all sterols.

 

Other Options:

  • Option A: Cyclopentano perhydro phenanthrene ring system – True. This is the core fused four-ring structure (3 cyclohexane rings + 1 cyclopentane) of all steroids, including cholesterol.
  • Option B: 3 cyclohexane rings – A, B and C –True. Rings A, B, and C in cholesterol are indeed cyclohexane rings, forming part of the classic steroid nucleus.
  • Option D: The OH group is beta oriented –True. The hydroxyl group on C-3 of cholesterol is oriented upward, i.e., beta orientation, which is above the plane of the ring system.

 

Educational Objective:


Understand the structural features of cholesterol, including its steroid nucleus (three cyclohexane + one cyclopentane ring), C-3 beta-hydroxyl group, and C-17 side chain. While cholesterol has an 8-carbon side chain at C-17, this is not shared by all sterols, which may have different modifications depending on function (e.g., hormones, bile acids, vitamin D).

questions.answerText: Short-term regulation by transcription of the gene for HMG CoA reductase
questions.solutionHtml:
ong>Explanation:

 

Cholesterol synthesis is tightly regulated at multiple levels, with HMG CoA reductase being the rate-limiting enzyme. 

 

Other Option:

 

Option A. Statins are competitive inhibitors of HMG CoA reductase: True.
Statins competitively inhibit HMG CoA reductase, reducing cholesterol synthesis and are widely used in hypercholesterolemia.

 

Option B. Insulin increases the activity of HMG CoA reductase: True.
Insulin promotes the dephosphorylation (activation) of HMG CoA reductase, enhancing cholesterol synthesis, especially in the fed state.

 

Option C. HMG CoA Reductase active in Fed State: True.
In the fed state, when insulin is high, cholesterol synthesis is active.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Understand the multi-level regulation of HMG-CoA reductase — the key control point in cholesterol biosynthesis — including:

  • Short-term (minutes): Phosphorylation/dephosphorylation
  • Long-term (hours–days): Gene transcription via SREBP
  • Drug intervention: Competitive inhibition by statins

questions.stem: Assertion (A): Bile acid protects the body from cholesterol over production. Reasoning (R): In liver, cholesterol is continuously converted to bile acid.

options.label: A
options.text: A and R both are right, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: A is wrong but R is a right statement

options.label: C
options.text: A as well as R are right, and R is a correct explanation of A

options.label: D
options.text: A and R both are wrong

questions.answerText: A as well as R are right, and R is a correct explanation of A
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>A as well as R are right, and R is a correct explanation of A

 

Option C:

 

Explanation:

 

Assertion (A) is correct. Bile acids, which are derived from cholesterol, play a significant role in maintaining cholesterol homeostasis within the body. By converting cholesterol into bile acids, the body can regulate the levels of cholesterol, preventing its overproduction and accumulation, which can lead to conditions such as hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis.

 

Reasoning (R) is also correct and provides a correct explanation for Assertion (A). The liver plays a crucial role in lipid metabolism, including the conversion of cholesterol into bile acids. This conversion is an important regulatory mechanism for controlling cholesterol levels in the body. Bile acids are then excreted into the intestine with bile, where they aid in the digestion and absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins. Some bile acids are reabsorbed from the intestine and returned to the liver, while others are lost in the feces. This loss of bile acids from the body necessitates the conversion of more cholesterol into bile acids, thus helping to regulate cholesterol levels and prevent overproduction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Bile acid production is the most important catabolic pathway for cholesterol.
  • Continuous conversation of cholesterol into bile acid in the liver prevents the body from becoming overloaded with cholesterol.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical researcher is developing a new class of lipid-lowering drugs aimed at targeting cholesterol biosynthesis. In a team meeting, he presents the biosynthetic pathway of cholesterol to identify potential targets for drug intervention. He highlights a crucial 30-carbon intermediate in the pathway and asks the team to identify this compound, emphasizing its significance in the synthesis of cholesterol:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Squalene

 

Option B:

 

  • In cholesterol biosynthesis, 6 numbers of 5-carbon units are condensed to form a 30-carbon compound known as Squalene.
  • Condensation of 5 Carbon isoprenoid units to form Squalene (30C):

 

 

  • Two 5C units condense to form a 10 C compound called as Geranyl Pyrophosphate.
  • 10C unit, Geranyl Pyrophosphate condenses with a 5C isoprenoid unit to form a 15C compound called Farnesyl Diphosphate.

 

 

  • Two Farnesyl Diphosphate (15C) condense to form a 30C compound called Squalene.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: 5C compound- Isoprenoid units

 

Option C: 10C compound- Geranyl Pyrophosphate.

 

Option D:  5C compound- Farnesyl Diphosphate.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Squalene is the correct answer as it is a 30-carbon compound that serves as a key intermediate in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway. Squalene is synthesized from the condensation of two farnesyl pyrophosphate molecules and is later cyclized to form lanosterol, which undergoes several modifications to become cholesterol.
